description: Applications the orchestrator could send, for local development. Every scenario is SIM-01 with one thing changed. The reason codes are the locked registry from api-contract.md §4 — do not invent new ones. Dates that must stay relative to today are written as {{today}} / {{today-18y}} / {{today-18y+1d}} tokens and resolved when the library loads, so no scenario can age out of testing what it claims to test.

scenarios.title: Happy path — rewards card
scenarios.trait: Nothing wrong with it. Every other scenario is this one with a single field changed.

scenarios.title: Happy path — standard card, second applicant
scenarios.trait: A second clean application, so not every green run is the same person and product.

scenarios.title: Age boundary — exactly 18 today
scenarios.trait: Turns 18 today, whenever today is. The pass side of the age boundary — 18 is old enough.
scenarios.note: Date of birth is {{today-18y}}, so the applicant is exactly 18 on the day you send it — this scenario can no longer age out. STUDENT minimum income is 0. DTI = 200 / (9000 / 12) = 0.267.

scenarios.title: Age boundary — one day short of 18
scenarios.trait: One day younger than scenario 03 and nothing else differs. The fail side of the boundary.
scenarios.note: Date of birth is {{today-18y+1d}} — one day too young, so 17 years 364 days on the day you send it. Paired with scenario 03: together they are both sides of the boundary, and neither drifts. (Before the tokens existed these were fixed dates, and scenario 04 quietly turned 18 the day after it was written.)

scenarios.title: Limit boundary — exactly the product maximum
scenarios.trait: Requests the top of the REWARDS band exactly. Inside the range, so it passes.

scenarios.title: Limit boundary — 500 over the product maximum
scenarios.trait: Same finances as 05, 500 over the band maximum. The fail side of the limit boundary.
scenarios.note: Two modules answer this differently and both are right: verification rejects it as outside 500-10 000, credit caps it to 10 000. That is ground rule 3 — steps are independent and never read each other's result.

scenarios.title: Terms and conditions not accepted
scenarios.trait: Everything is well-formed and affordable; the customer simply never ticked the box.
scenarios.note: consents.termsAccepted is false. Module 1 rejects on it; module 6 cannot raise an agreement without it.

scenarios.title: Required fields missing
scenarios.trait: A well-formed envelope carrying an incomplete application: three fields are null.
scenarios.note: Null, not empty string — contract §3: optional fields are omitted or null, never "" or 0. Your module must say WHICH field is missing in the reason detail.

scenarios.title: Field formats invalid
scenarios.trait: Every value is present and every one is in the wrong shape.
scenarios.note: Five format breaks: date of birth DD/MM/YYYY not YYYY-MM-DD, email has no @, mobile is not E.164, country codes are alpha-3 and lower case not ISO alpha-2 upper, expiry date reversed. Contract §3 ground rules on values.

scenarios.title: Tax residency on the excluded list (US)
scenarios.trait: Dual tax residency, one of them the one country the bank will not onboard.
scenarios.note: Contract §3: excluded list is US. Note taxResidencies is an array — a module that only reads the first entry passes this one by mistake. DTI = (1400 + 200) / (52000 / 12) = 1600 / 4333.33 = 0.369.

scenarios.title: Tax residency not on the supported list (BR)
scenarios.trait: Not excluded, just not supported — a different answer from scenario 10 on purpose.
scenarios.note: Supported list is GB, IE, PL, DE, FR, ES, NL. BR is on neither list, which is not the same as being on the excluded one — two reason codes, two situations.

scenarios.title: Existing customer applying for a second card
scenarios.trait: The same human as SIM-01 — same name, date of birth and email — under a new application id.
scenarios.note: Send SIM-01 first, then this one. Module 2 must key its one-card-per-customer rule on the person, not on applicationId — this scenario is the only thing that tells you whether it does.

scenarios.title: Identity document expired
scenarios.trait: Clean in every other respect; the passport ran out eight months ago.
scenarios.note: Expiry 2025-11-30, a literal date on purpose: a document that has expired stays expired, so this one cannot drift and does not need a token. Your mock ID provider should not need to be called to answer it — the date is enough.

scenarios.title: ID provider unavailable
scenarios.trait: The integration failure every mock needs a way to reproduce on demand.
scenarios.note: Corpus convention: a documentId of ZZ0000000 means 'make your mock provider fail'. Wire your mock to time out or 503 on it. Module 3 exists to teach a failure mode — this is the input that lets you demonstrate it without unplugging anything.

scenarios.title: Sanctions list — exact name match
scenarios.trait: The name your screening fixture list must contain, spelled exactly.
scenarios.note: Corpus convention: Viktor Petrov, born 1975-05-14, is the planted exact hit. Put him on your mock watchlist. DTI = (2200 + 400) / (88000 / 12) = 2600 / 7333.33 = 0.355 — affordable, so only screening should stop this one.

scenarios.title: Sanctions list — partial name match
scenarios.trait: A different, innocent person whose name is close to the planted hit.
scenarios.note: Same stem as scenario 15, different first name and a different date of birth. A partial match is a referral for a human to clear, not a rejection — this is the pair that shows your matching is fuzzy but your decision is not.

scenarios.title: High-risk country
scenarios.trait: Nobody on any list; the country of the nationality and the document is the trigger.
scenarios.note: nationality and identityDocument.issuingCountry are IR while countryOfResidence is GB. Which field your rule reads is a design decision — write it down.

scenarios.title: Income below the product minimum
scenarios.trait: Affordable but under the product's income floor — one rule fails, the other passes.
scenarios.note: REWARDS minimum income is 20 000; this is 18 000. Affordability is fine: DTI = (500 + 50) / (18000 / 12) = 550 / 1500 = 0.367. A module that only checks DTI lets this through.

scenarios.title: Affordability boundary — DTI 0.44
scenarios.trait: Just inside the affordability limit. The pass side of the DTI boundary.

scenarios.title: Affordability boundary — DTI 0.46
scenarios.trait: 50 pounds a month more in commitments than scenario 19, and nothing else.
scenarios.note: DTI = (1000 + 150) / (30000 / 12) = 1150 / 2500 = 0.460 > 0.45. The 50-pound difference from scenario 19 is the whole test: rounding or > vs >= shows up here.

scenarios.title: Card delivered to a different address
scenarios.trait: Moved in four months ago and wants the card sent to work — the delivery branch nobody tests.
scenarios.note: delivery.useCurrentAddress is false, so module 8 must post to delivery.address and not to applicant.currentAddress. DTI = 1500 / (47000 / 12) = 1500 / 3916.67 = 0.383.

scenarios.title: Alternate delivery requested, no address given
scenarios.trait: The contradictory combination — do not use the current address, and here is no other one.
scenarios.note: The pair to scenario 21. A module that reads delivery.address without checking for null throws here instead of answering, and a thrown module never calls back.

scenarios.title: Unknown fields must be ignored
scenarios.trait: A clean application carrying three fields your module has never heard of.
scenarios.note: Contract §3: unknown fields are ignored on the way in and never emitted on the way out. This scenario passes only if your parsing does not fail on campaignCode, referrer, applicant.middleName and product.promoRate. It is how the contract grows without breaking you.

scenarios.title: Unknown product code (the b00 demo generator's)
scenarios.trait: A product code that is not in the locked catalogue — because the running orchestrator still sends it.
scenarios.note: Tracked drift: attempt-b00's demo generator emits CREDIT_CARD_PREMIUM and CREDIT_CARD_PLATINUM; the locked catalogue in api-contract.md §3 has STANDARD, REWARDS and STUDENT. Your module must not crash on a code it does not know. Decide what it does and write it down — referring for a human is a defensible answer.

scenarios.title: The same application id, sent twice
scenarios.trait: SIM-01 again, with a changed credit limit — the orchestrator retrying a dispatch.
scenarios.note: Send scenario 01 first. This is a re-send of the SAME applicationId: the module must answer 202 again and must NOT create a second row (RequestService.receive reuses the existing one). Watch what happens to the stored payload — the template keeps the first one. Decide whether that is what you want.

scenarios.title: Invalid envelope — no application id
scenarios.trait: Not an application at all: the one field the envelope cannot do without is absent.
scenarios.note: The only scenario that must NOT return 202. @NotBlank on ApplicationRequest.applicationId makes this a 400 with the error shape from ApiExceptionHandler, and nothing is written to the database. If your module answers 202 here, your validation is gone.
